idiom_name: CryptoKit AES.GCM.SealedBox over an encoded protected map + hand-written Codable/CustomStringConvertible
implementation_notes: CryptoKit supplies the sealing primitive directly: AES.GCM.seal(_:using:) returns a SealedBox (nonce, ciphertext and tag, combined) and AES.GCM.open verifies and decrypts with a SymmetricKey, so the transfer object stores the combined bytes and implements Codable by hand - synthesized conformance writes every stored property, so encode(to:)/init(from:) must be written to emit only the sealed box. CustomStringConvertible and CustomDebugStringConvertible keep print, interpolation, dump and debugger views away from the plaintext. What replaces the classic structure: the hand-written Codable conformance replaces the serialized data map and description replaces the masked-list rendering, while key handling is a value-type SymmetricKey rather than a framework service.
pitfalls: Synthesized Codable includes every stored property regardless of access level: a private plaintext field is still encoded unless encode(to:)/init(from:) are hand-written, and adding a field silently changes the wire form.

print/String(describing:) uses description only when the type conforms to CustomStringConvertible; otherwise the default reflection prints all stored properties, so conform explicitly (and to CustomDebugStringConvertible for dump()/debugger).

AES.GCM.SealedBox(combined:) expects CryptoKit's own layout (nonce, ciphertext, tag); payloads sealed elsewhere need the explicit initializer, and a failed tag check throws - treat it as tampering, never as an empty map.
SymmetricKey is a value type that can be copied and CryptoKit does not guarantee zeroization of arbitrary buffers; keep plaintext lifetimes short and never store the key inside the transfer object.
